channel.description: Balanced Information, Actual Stories. Biased toward calm.

item.title: New songbook captures 'living collection of our unofficial national anthems'
item.description:
Australia has launched a National Songbook, a new initiative designed to celebrate and preserve the songs that have shaped the nation's cultural identity. The project, a collaboration between the National Film and Sound Archive and music rights organization APRA AMCOS, honors compositions that have become unofficial national anthems—songs that capture who Australians are, where they've been, and where they hope to go.
The first ten inductees span more than a century and traverse diverse genres and perspectives. They range from the 1890s bush ballad "Waltzing Matilda" to The Presets' 2007 electronic anthem "My People." The collection includes protest songs like Midnight Oil's "Beds Are Burning" and Yothu Yindi's landmark "Treaty," Helen Reddy's feminist rallying cry "I Am Woman," and deeply personal works like Ruby Hunter's "Down City Streets." Also recognized are The Easybeats' global hit "Friday On My Mind," the evocative "My Island Home," Peter Sculthorpe's orchestral piece "Earth Cry," and The Necks' atmospheric film soundtrack. A panel of ten music experts, academics, and journalists guided the selections, emphasizing artistic merit and cultural resonance over commercial success alone.
Unlike existing collections that focus on specific recordings, the National Songbook celebrates the songs themselves—the compositions that endure across different versions, generations, and contexts. It's conceived as an evolving conversation rather than a fixed canon, with new inductees planned annually. For a nation still exploring its identity, this living archive offers something quietly profound: a way to hear the many voices and stories that make up the Australian experience, preserved not just as sound, but as memory and meaning.

item.title: Trust vows to 'maintain spirit' of nature reserve
item.description:
A beloved wildlife garden in Suffolk has found a new guardian after a period of uncertainty. Flatford Wildlife Garden, near East Bergholt, faced an unclear future last October when the RSPB announced it would need to sell or lease the property due to financial constraints. This week, the National Trust officially took ownership, ensuring the site will continue to welcome visitors and support local biodiversity.
The garden, originally a legacy gift to the RSPB from sisters Sylvia and Margaret Richardson about fifteen years ago, has been managed by the organization since 2011. It features wildlife trails with carved wooden creatures, a living willow tunnel, a pond, and insect hotels designed to support pollinators and other small fauna. Previously open only during summer months, the National Trust plans to prepare the site over winter for a spring reopening, aiming for early March or before Easter. The acquisition was made possible through support and funding from local community groups, reflecting the garden's importance to the area.
This story offers a quiet reminder of how conservation efforts can adapt and endure through collaboration. The National Trust has pledged to maintain the garden's character while exploring ways to better integrate it with the broader Flatford site and improve accessibility. For those who value community-centered green spaces and the careful stewardship of nature, this transition represents not just the preservation of a special place, but a testament to what can happen when organizations and communities work together to protect what matters locally.

item.title: Collins Dictionary names 'mogging' its word of the year
item.description:
Collins Dictionary has crowned "mogging" — meaning to upstage or outperform someone or something — as its 2026 word of the year, marking a 210 percent increase in usage over the past twelve months. The term, which evolved from bodybuilding culture around 2016 and the acronym AMOG ("alpha male of the group"), has migrated from niche online spaces into everyday conversation, where it now describes everything from a teenager outshining an elite athlete to one friend's sourdough loaf putting another's to shame.
The word's journey reflects both the linguistic creativity and the concerns of the social media age. While it began in what researchers call "the manosphere," where some influencers have used questionable formulas to rank people's attractiveness in hierarchical terms, the word has broken free of those origins. Sociology researcher Simon Copland notes the troubling quantitative measures sometimes associated with the concept, particularly regarding their impact on young men. Yet lexicographers observe that "mogging" has become ubiquitous across contexts, shedding much of its original baggage as it entered mainstream use.
This story offers a window into how language evolves in real time, shaped by online communities before spilling into broader culture. The shortlist of other contenders — from "bixie" haircuts to "ghost jobs" and "p(doom)" — reveals the preoccupations and playfulness of our moment. It's a reminder that dictionaries aren't just guardians of static meaning but witnesses to the living, breathing shifts in how we communicate, compete, and make sense of the world around us.

item.title: Excitement as albatross lays egg on Dunedin livestream
item.description:
A royal albatross known simply as L has given viewers around the world a front-row seat to something rarely witnessed: the moment she laid the very first egg of the season at New Zealand's Pukekura/Taiaroa Head colony. The event unfolded live on Sunday via the Royal Cam, a livestream partnership between the Department of Conservation and Cornell University's Lab of Ornithology that attracts millions of viewers annually. When DOC ranger Sharyn Broni checked the feed after waking to hundreds of excited comments, she was amazed by what she saw—and heard. L was, she noted, unusually vocal during the process.
The albatross, who skipped building her own nest and instead recycled one from the previous season, is now sharing incubation duties with her mate. The egg will be monitored in about ten days to confirm whether it's fertile, and if all goes well, the chick will hatch after roughly 79 days. Since Sunday, four more eggs have been laid at the colony, marking a hopeful continuation of a remarkable conservation success story. Just this past season, a record-tying 38 chicks fledged from Pukekura—a dramatic increase from the roughly ten fledglings per year three decades ago.
This story offers a quiet testament to patience and partnership. The colony is co-managed by the Pukekura Co-management Trust, blending the efforts of Te Rūnanga o Ōtākou, local councils, and conservation groups. The livestream does more than document; it invites connection with a taonga species, helping people across the globe feel invested in the survival of these magnificent seabirds. It's a reminder that sometimes the most meaningful moments unfold slowly, one carefully tended egg at a time.

item.title: New museum's garden artwork recovered four lost First Nations words
item.description:
A new art installation at Sydney's Powerhouse Parramatta is quietly correcting a historical injustice that erased an Indigenous man's contributions to early Australian botany. Daniel Moowattin, a Burramattagal man who worked with British botanist George Caley in the early 1800s, was the person actually collecting plant specimens—climbing trees and gathering clippings—yet his name was systematically removed from official records. While Caley's personal herbarium notes acknowledged Moowattin's work with handwritten annotations like "got by Dan," these attributions vanished when the records were formalized, leaving Moowattin largely forgotten.
Artist Keg de Souza and Dharug elder Uncle Chris Tobin traced Moowattin's footsteps, collecting eucalyptus clippings from the same country where he once worked. Curator Emerson Radisich spent months searching archives worldwide, eventually finding about 100 herbarium sheets at London's Natural History Museum. Among these records, the team discovered handwritten notations in the Dharug language—including four words related to eucalyptus species that had been lost to time. One word, Dhuramba (the name for Eucalyptus Paniculata), has been confirmed, with three others awaiting formal publication.
The bronze plaques now embedded in the museum's rooftop garden do more than commemorate one man's overlooked work. They represent a broader reckoning with how Indigenous knowledge has been appropriated and erased. As Uncle Chris observed seeing the installation for the first time, it helps people understand that Aboriginal history isn't just part of Parramatta's story—it's foundational to it. This quiet act of recovery reminds us that behind many scientific achievements are untold collaborators whose contributions deserve recognition.

item.title: Handball athletes from Fernando de Noronha are welcomed with celebration after victories
item.description:
A women's handball team from Fernando de Noronha, a remote Brazilian island, returned home to a joyful celebration after winning the under-18 championship and placing second in the under-16 category at a regional North-Northeast tournament. The young athletes, all students from the island's Escola Arquipélago, were greeted with a fire truck escort from the airport and cheered by fellow students at their school—a moment of pride for a community where such opportunities are rare.
The team competed in Campina Grande against rivals from across northern Brazil, including finalists from Ceará. The under-18 squad went undefeated through six matches, while the under-16 team lost only once. Coach Isaac Lira, who has run a handball program on the island for nine years, emphasized how meaningful it is for his players to compete beyond their isolated home. For these sixteen young women, the tournament offered more than trophies—it was a chance to travel, face new challenges, and build friendships with athletes from other regions.
What makes this story quietly remarkable is the way a small island community has built something meaningful around sport. Goalkeeper Clara Luine and player Maia Moreno both spoke of the experience with gratitude, highlighting not just victory but growth, connection, and fun. Coach Lira sees the homecoming celebration as vital for inspiring the next generation of island athletes, proving that geographic isolation needn't mean limited horizons. It's a reminder that community investment in young people—through sport, recognition, and opportunity—can resonate far beyond the scoreboard.

item.title: Kick Back report exposes extent, causes of youth homelessness
item.description:
A youth charity in New Zealand is witnessing a sharp rise in young people experiencing homelessness, with some as young as 11 sleeping rough on city streets. Kick Back, which operates a youth hub on Auckland's Karangahape Road, has released its second 'State of the Street' report showing a 95 percent increase in referrals over the past year. The findings reveal that 73 percent of young people accessing their services are either sleeping rough or couch surfing—up from 44 percent in the previous report. Family breakdown emerges as a leading cause, with nearly a third of young people reporting they left home due to violence, abuse, or feeling unsafe.
The report brings faces to the statistics. Frankie, now in his early twenties, first became homeless at age 11 after losing his father and struggling in foster care. He lived in places like cemeteries for a decade before connecting with Kick Back, and now helps other young people navigating similar circumstances. The charity's hub offers immediate support—showers, clean clothes, food—and helps secure emergency accommodation, though many young people cycle between temporary housing and the streets.
This story matters because it reveals a crisis hiding in plain sight in New Zealand's cities, affecting children at ages when they should be in school and safely housed. The report's twelve recommendations, including duty-to-assist legislation and restoring benefit access for 18-19 year olds, suggest systemic solutions exist. What makes this quietly remarkable is the resilience of young people like Frankie and the community forming around Kick Back's work—people determined to ensure others don't face the same struggles alone.

item.title: Brazil election sparks threats to reinvade Indigenous Amazon territory
item.description:
In October 2023, a federal judge in Brazil ordered emergency deployment of security forces to the Apyterewa Indigenous Land in Pará state after evidence surfaced of a planned reinvasion by hundreds of former non-Indigenous occupants. The timing coincided with Brazil's presidential runoff election, and WhatsApp messages documented threats suggesting the invaders expected political support depending on the election's outcome. Audio recordings warned the Parakanã Indigenous people to leave, with references to potential gunfire and claims that newly elected officials would "release the land to white people."
The threats reflect deeper tensions over Indigenous territories in the Amazon. During Jair Bolsonaro's presidency from 2019 to 2023, Apyterewa became Brazil's most deforested Indigenous territory, losing over 30,000 hectares to illegal logging and cattle ranching. After Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won the election and took office in 2023, federal agencies successfully removed non-Indigenous invaders who had occupied the land for years. Federal prosecutors note that political rhetoric from opposition leaders who oppose Indigenous land demarcation has directly endangered Indigenous communities, emboldening those who view territorial protections as negotiable based on election results.
This story quietly illuminates how Indigenous land rights remain vulnerable to political winds, and how digital platforms can amplify threats into coordinated action. The successful deployment of security forces prevented the planned invasion, but the incident underscores an ongoing struggle where the safety of Indigenous peoples and the preservation of critical rainforest habitat hang in the balance of electoral politics and enforcement capacity.

item.title: 'Glory to God. Finally the blessing arrived': residents of Mojuí dos Campos celebrate rain after drought and wildfires
item.description:
In the rural communities of Mojuí dos Campos, a municipality in western Pará, Brazil, residents greeted Monday night's rainfall with tears of gratitude and prayers of thanksgiving. After enduring severe drought, choking smoke from wildfires, and extreme heat, families filmed themselves celebrating as drops drummed on their roofs. "Glory to God! Finally the blessing has arrived," one resident exclaimed in a video that captured the relief washing over the Castanheira and São Francisco communities.
The rain arrived at a critical moment. Just weeks earlier, local authorities had declared a level-two state of emergency affecting 3,100 rural residents facing water shortages. The relentless dry season had drained streams, springs, small reservoirs, and even artesian wells that communities depend on. Family farms suffered irreparable losses as crops withered and pastures dried up, leaving animals struggling to find food. October alone brought 440 wildfire hotspots detected by satellite, blanketing the region in smoke and ash.
While the rainfall offered welcome respite from the immediate crisis, forecasters caution it's not enough to reverse the historic drought gripping the Amazon. Temperatures are expected to climb back to 36–38°C, with only isolated showers predicted. This story captures a moment of profound human emotion in the face of environmental crisis—a reminder that what many take for granted can become a blessing worth celebrating, and that hope persists even when relief is partial and the challenges remain daunting.

item.title: Pediatric palliative care addresses the unique needs of seriously ill children and their families
item.description:
Pediatric palliative care is a specialized field that addresses a reality many find difficult to contemplate: children facing serious, life-limiting illnesses. This approach emerged in the 1990s and early 2000s, adapting the adult hospice model to meet the distinct needs of young patients and their families. Rather than simply managing end-of-life care, it focuses on making every day as meaningful as possible, whether a child has months or years remaining.
The care model brings together physicians, nurses, social workers, chaplains, and other specialists who work as a team to address physical, emotional, social, and spiritual needs. Research over the past two decades shows tangible benefits: children experience less pain and fewer distressing symptoms, and families receive crucial support in navigating complex medical decisions. For instance, when a palliative care team is involved, families are better equipped to choose treatments that genuinely improve quality of life rather than prolonging suffering. This holistic approach also helps ensure that intensive care interventions align with a family's actual goals, rather than defaulting to every possible medical intervention regardless of outcome.
While nearly 80% of U.S. children's hospitals now have formal palliative care programs—making America a leader in this field—access remains inconsistent, particularly outside hospital settings. Globally, with an estimated 7 million children dying annually, the need far exceeds availability. This story matters because it illuminates a compassionate, evidence-based approach to one of life's most difficult experiences, reminding us that even in the face of profound loss, care can focus on comfort, dignity, and moments of joy.

item.title: What is the 'zeptoverse,' the smallest world ever detected in nature and why it is key to understanding the universe
item.description:
Scientists have detected signals from the smallest scale of nature ever explored — a realm 100 billion times smaller than an atom that some physicists are calling the "zeptoverse." The discovery, made by Cambridge-based researchers using the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, represents the culmination of more than 40 years of searching and could open new pathways to understanding dark matter and the fundamental workings of the universe.
The breakthrough centers on observing an extremely rare decay of the bottom quark, a subatomic particle that exists for only 1.5 trillionths of a second before disintegrating. Researchers managed to detect its interactions with other tiny particles at a scale of one billionth of a meter. At these minuscule dimensions, particles may be more sensitive to dark matter, the mysterious substance that makes up much of our cosmos but remains invisible except through its gravitational effects. Dr. Harry Cliff, who led the data analysis, described the work as "knocking on the door of the zeptoverse," explaining that this subatomic dance gives researchers a privileged view of how potential new particles behave.
This story offers a glimpse into the patient, decades-long work of pushing the boundaries of human knowledge into realms almost impossible to imagine. It reminds us that understanding the universe sometimes means looking not outward into the vastness of space, but inward into the inconceivably small — where the answers to cosmic mysteries may quietly wait to be discovered, one billionth of a trillionth of a meter at a time.

item.title: After 1 year hospitalized, teenager who had 90% of body burned in explosion returns home: 'His eyes shine with joy,' says mother
item.description:
After seventeen months in a hospital in Catanduva, Brazil, fourteen-year-old Rikelme Alexandre de Brito has returned home, marking a milestone in his recovery from burns covering nearly 90% of his body. The injuries occurred on Easter Sunday 2025, when a backyard barbecue ignited unexpectedly due to alcohol used to light the fire. The explosion injured Rikelme, his younger brother Maxwell, and their mother Lucimari. While Rikelme survived after extensive treatment including multiple surgeries and skin grafts, seven-year-old Maxwell did not.
Rikelme's journey has been marked by physical pain and the emotional weight of his brother's death, with his mother describing how depression set in during the long hospital stay. Yet the moment he received clearance to go home, the family's prayers and patience found their answer. Lucimari says the change in her son has been immediate and profound—he sleeps better, feels no pain, and most tellingly, his eyes now shine with joy rather than suffering. He still wears compression bandages around the clock and will need additional surgeries as his skin continues to heal, with no set timeline yet established.
This story offers a quiet testament to resilience and the healing power of home. It reminds us that recovery isn't measured only in medical procedures, but in the return of light to a child's eyes, in the comfort of familiar walls, and in a mother's relief at having her son near after months of uncertainty and loss. It's a story about survival, yes, but also about what comes after—the slow, hopeful work of rebuilding a life.

item.title: Christchurch teen wins $400,000 scholarship to Berklee music college
item.description:
A Christchurch teenager who first felt the thrill of performing while playing Guns N' Roses at a primary school concert has won a full scholarship worth $400,000 to study at Boston's prestigious Berklee College of Music. Corban Blackwell, now 17, began his musical journey at age eight with a three-quarter-size acoustic guitar from his grandmother, but it was the electric guitar that truly ignited his passion around age 11. Today, he practices up to five hours daily in his bedroom, favoring a headless seven-string electric guitar that allows him to play faster melodies.
Corban's dedication has already yielded remarkable results. Last year, his Burnside High School band Equilibrium made history as the first instrumental act to win the national Smokefreerockquest title, a turning point that made a music career feel genuinely possible. His playing style blends the technical precision of rock and metal with the harmonic complexity of jazz, influenced heavily by Tim Henson of the instrumental band Polyphia. The scholarship came after Corban attended Berklee's summer program and successfully auditioned while in the United States.
This story captures something quietly extraordinary about dedication and craft. It's a reminder that passion, when nurtured with discipline and support from family, school, and community, can open doors to world-class opportunities. For a teenager who once felt like he was "shredding to everyone in the world" at a school concert, that feeling is about to become much closer to reality.

item.title: Peacock found in couple’s Brisbane bathroom leads to creative bid to reunite bird with tattoo artist
item.description:
A peacock named Hex made an unexpected entrance into a Brisbane couple's home, where they discovered him transfixed by his own reflection in their bathroom mirror. Geoff and Delwyn Ballantyne returned from an evening coffee to find the fully grown bird had wandered in through their open garage door and taken up residence admiring himself. After wildlife rescuers relocated Hex to nearby bushland, he began making afternoon visits to another Alexandra Hills property, where the owner connected the dots and identified him as belonging to local tattoo artist Elliot Ross.
The story took a creative turn when the property owner, Suzie Tafolo, Googled peacock-catching techniques and learned about their fondness for mirrors. She strategically placed a full-length mirror in her back shed, hoping to lure Hex long enough for a reunion with his owner. Ross, who has owned the bird for a couple of years, suspects Hex might be searching for additional female company, as the peacock has a mate back home who stayed put during his adventure.
Urban ecologist Darryl Jones suggests Hex's mirror fixation might stem from loneliness rather than vanity, noting that while most birds perceive their reflection as a rival to fight, this peacock may simply be seeking companionship. It's a gently absurd tale that reminds us how wildlife adapts to suburban landscapes in unexpected ways, and how a community can come together with equal parts humor and ingenuity to solve the delightfully unusual problem of a lovesick—or perhaps just lonely—peacock on the loose.

item.title: Meet the Englishman who came home after walking around the world for 28 years
item.description:
Karl Bushby left England in 1998 with $500 in his pocket and an improbable plan: to walk home from Chile without using any motorized transport. Twenty-eight years later, the former British paratrooper completed his journey, covering nearly 50,000 kilometers across 29 countries on foot and by swimming. He started in Punta Arenas, trekked through the Americas for eight years, crossed the frozen Bering Strait in 2006, spent 18 years traversing Asia, and finally returned to his hometown of Hull this week, greeted by his mother for the first time in nearly three decades.
The journey was born from a casual conversation among military friends who doubted anyone could cross the Bering Strait. Bushby set out to prove them wrong and kept going. Along the way, he faced bureaucratic obstacles that delayed him a decade in Russia alone, endured pandemic lockdowns, illness, extreme weather, and stretches of open water including 300 kilometers in the Caspian Sea and the English Channel. Strangers offered food and shelter throughout, and he pushed a cart containing basic survival gear across continents.
What makes this story quietly remarkable isn't just the physical feat, but Bushby's conclusion after three decades circling the globe. He found the world "extraordinarily good," encountering the best of humanity 99% of the time across every culture and country. Now 57, he plans to reconnect with his son, meet his 12-year-old granddaughter, and find steady work—no more epic adventures. It's a testament to human endurance, kindness, and the surprising goodness waiting beyond our borders.

item.title: The emotional homecoming of Karl Bushby, the British adventurer who walked around the world after departing from Chile 28 years ago
item.description:
After 28 years of walking, Karl Bushby has completed one of the most extraordinary journeys in modern exploration history. The 57-year-old British adventurer crossed the Humber Bridge through thick fog on Monday, marking the end of a 49,890-kilometer trek that began in Punta Arenas, Chile, in 1998. His self-imposed rules were simple but uncompromising: walk home to Hull, England, without using any motorized transport, and don't return until the journey is complete.
What started as a personal reset following a difficult divorce stretched from an estimated 12 years into nearly three decades. Bushby encountered visa restrictions, lost sponsors during the 2008 financial crisis, weathered the COVID-19 pandemic, and navigated geopolitical complexities. His route took him through four continents: north through the Americas, across the frozen Bering Strait into Russia, through Siberia and Central Asia, swimming 300 kilometers across the Caspian Sea, and finally into Europe. Along the way, he pushed "La Bestia"—his shopping cart companion he affectionately compared to the volleyball Wilson from the film "Cast Away."
Bushby was met by cheering crowds, his mother, and filmmaker Werner Herzog, who plans to document the journey. What makes this story quietly remarkable is not just the physical feat, but Bushby's humility throughout—describing himself as "just a homeless person pushing a shopping cart" while recognizing the profound meaning his perseverance holds for others. It's a testament to human determination and the transformative power of setting a course and following through, no matter how long the road.

item.title: Call to heaven: Action with telephone awakens memories and moves visitors at cemetery in Acre; VIDEO
item.description:
In the small town of Feijó, in Brazil's Acre state, a simple vintage telephone became a bridge between the living and the departed. On All Souls' Day, Father Cleiton Silveira placed the old phone at the entrance of Santa Cecília Cemetery, inviting visitors to "call heaven and speak with someone special." What unfolded was a profoundly moving display of grief, love, and connection as people lined up to leave voice messages for loved ones who had passed.
The idea emerged from Father Silveira's own experience with loss—his mother died just three months before his ordination, never seeing him become a priest, and his grandmother passed earlier this year. He still records voice messages for his mother and listens to old WhatsApp audio recordings of their conversations. Wanting to offer something deeply human in an age of artificial intelligence, he created this analog space for mourning. Between 15 and 20 people participated, sharing messages that ranged from everyday updates to expressions of enduring sorrow. One woman spoke to her father and asked him to tell Nahyure—a 21-year-old who died in an August traffic accident—that she was missed. Another mother tearfully told her son how much his absence still hurts.
This story matters because it captures something rarely seen: grief given voice in a public, compassionate space. The pastoral communication team filming the event found themselves crying alongside participants, witnessing how a pretend phone call could genuinely ease suffering. In its beautiful simplicity, the telephone offered what technology often promises but seldom delivers—a moment of real human connection, and perhaps, a small measure of peace.

item.title: Diverse forests can better withstand extreme weather events, study finds. Here’s why
item.description:
A sweeping new study of American forests offers a hopeful finding for a warming world: woodlands with a greater variety of tree species are better equipped to survive and bounce back from the compound climate extremes that are becoming increasingly common. Researchers analyzed nearly 90,000 forest plots across the continental United States, examining how different ecosystems responded when multiple stressors struck simultaneously—such as severe drought paired with extreme heat, or heat waves combined with unusually heavy rainfall.
Using satellite imagery to track forest "greenness" during and after climate events, the team discovered that diverse forests maintained photosynthesis more effectively under stress and recovered more quickly afterward. The combination of heat and drought proved especially challenging, causing more dramatic impacts than the sum of these stressors occurring separately. What makes this research particularly significant is its scale: while previous studies had hinted at diversity's protective effects in smaller experimental plots, this work confirms the pattern holds true across vast, complex natural ecosystems—a finding that genuinely surprised lead researcher Xuetao Qiao.
The study also revealed important nuances. Diversity's protective power varied depending on the type of climate event, and other factors like soil quality and baseline rainfall remained influential. Still, for forest managers facing an uncertain climate future, the research offers practical guidance: nurturing a mix of tree species may be one of the most effective strategies for building resilience. In an era of intersecting environmental pressures, this quietly remarkable study reminds us that nature's own diversity might be among our best defenses.

item.title: Molecular traces from 'blood cells' found in 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones
item.description:
Scientists studying the fossilized bones of a 115-million-year-old Brazilian dinosaur have reported finding molecular traces of heme—a key component of hemoglobin that carries oxygen in red blood cells. The discovery, made by a team led by Curtin University's Kliti Grice, was found within ellipsoid structures in the vascular canals of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a feathered dinosaur estimated to have been about four years old when it died. According to Professor Grice, this marks the first time anyone has detected heme inside a fossil blood cell, opening new avenues for understanding dinosaur metabolism and physiology.
The remarkable preservation may have been aided by microbial mats—colonies of bacteria and archaea common in coastal environments—that engulfed the dinosaur's remains. The researchers believe that conditions created by these microorganisms, including oxidation and simultaneous mineralization, helped preserve soft tissue over millions of years. The bones, discovered in a Brazilian mine in 2008, were analyzed using multiple techniques including electron microscopy and mass spectrometry. Surprisingly, the samples were found to be nearly 80 percent heme, though tests for ancient DNA came back negative.
While the findings add to growing evidence that soft tissue can survive in dinosaur fossils longer than once thought possible, some experts remain cautious. Not all scientists are convinced the structures definitively represent red blood cells, noting that interpretation is still required when examining chemical remnants and mineralized shapes. Still, even skeptics acknowledge the presence of heme and collagen is remarkable. The study offers a glimpse into how ancient life might be preserved in unexpected ways, and researchers are now testing whether similar fossilization could occur with human blood in microbial mats from Western Australia.

item.title: Zanzibar’s seaweed farmers see better future through science and partnership (commentary)
item.description:
Along the shores of Zanzibar, thousands of women wade into the ocean with the tides, cultivating seaweed that has sustained their families and communities for decades. This quiet, labor-intensive work connects the Tanzanian island to global markets and provides vital income to coastal households. Now, as climate change and environmental pressures reshape marine ecosystems worldwide, a collaborative effort involving the Zanzibar government, the United Nations, and international NGOs is working to secure the future of this vital industry through science and partnership.
The challenge is subtle but significant. For years, farmers have propagated existing stocks of Kappaphycus seaweed, locally called "cottonii." Over time, this practice may have gradually reduced genetic diversity, making cultivated varieties more vulnerable as ocean temperatures rise. Higher-value seaweed that once flourished in shallow waters has become harder to grow, affecting farmers' earnings. But recent research offers hope: naturally occurring populations of the seaweed still exist in Tanzanian waters, and early findings suggest they may carry traits for disease resistance and heat tolerance that could strengthen future cultivation.
This isn't a story of environmental crisis alone—it's a story of possibility. The partnership seeks to weave scientific innovation into the deep traditional knowledge these women already hold. Rather than viewing the farmers as the problem, the initiative recognizes them as the industry's greatest asset. It's a reminder that preserving livelihoods in a changing world often means honoring what's already there while carefully introducing tools that can help it endure.

item.title: Rare ant nest stolen from last place in England where species survives
item.description:
A colony of narrow-headed ants—possibly containing up to 5,000 individuals and several breeding queens—has been stolen from a nature reserve in Devon, the only place in England where this rare species still survives. Conservation researchers discovered the theft in mid-October when they found a suspicious hole where a known nest had been, along with clear evidence of digging. The loss represents a significant setback for a species that has declined dramatically over the past century due to habitat loss from agriculture and development.
Narrow-headed ants, named for their distinctively "pinched" heads, were once common across southern heathlands but are now classified as nationally rare and near threatened. Each colony develops slowly, and the queens can live for up to 25 years, meaning a mature nest represents decades of growth that cannot easily be replaced. Conservationists believe the thief likely had specialized knowledge, as ant nests are not obvious to casual observers. The motive remains unclear, though possibilities include a misguided rewilding attempt or collection by an insect enthusiast. Devon Wildlife Trust emphasized that properly relocating ants requires considerable expertise and careful preparation—work they had been planning themselves as part of long-term recovery efforts.
This story quietly underscores how even the smallest creatures face pressures from human activity, and how fragile the last threads of biodiversity can be. It's a reminder that conservation work often unfolds over years and generations, and that setbacks—whether from development or theft—can undo careful stewardship in moments. The loss of a single nest might seem minor, but for England's last population of narrow-headed ants, it's a meaningful blow to survival.

item.title: At 96, retired teacher fulfills dream of launching first book at Porto Alegre Book Fair: 'There's always time'
item.description:
At 96 years old, retired teacher Ema Vargas has published her first book at the Porto Alegre Book Fair in Brazil, proving that creative dreams know no age limit. Her collection, "I Come to Offer My Heart," gathers more than a hundred poems handwritten in a memory notebook throughout her lifetime. The work reflects her personal philosophy that time should never be seen as a barrier to living fully.
Ema's verses explore themes of aging, human relationships, and the passage of time with sincerity and warmth. In one poem, she writes to Time itself, asking for honesty in their relationship. In another, she reflects on how sharing affection can smooth the thorns along life's path. Beyond writing, Ema maintains her vitality by dancing tango in her spare time, a detail that delights her family. Her daughter, a psychologist, expresses joy at her mother's continued life force and energy at such an advanced age.
This story resonates because it challenges common assumptions about creativity, productivity, and what's possible in later life. Ema actively encourages others who feel limited by age to embrace a more positive outlook, rejecting generational labels entirely. When asked if she plans to continue writing, her response is simple and hopeful: "Yes, God willing." It's a quiet reminder that inspiration and purpose can flourish at any stage of life, and that the act of creating something meaningful can bring profound joy regardless of when it happens.

item.title: Jo Marchant: In search of now
item.description:
What does it mean to experience 'now'? It's a question that seems simple on the surface, yet becomes wonderfully complicated when examined from multiple perspectives. UK science writer Jo Marchant recently explored this deceptively tricky concept in a talk at London's Royal Institution, drawing from research for her upcoming book In Search of Now.
Marchant takes listeners on an intellectual journey across disciplines, weaving together insights from philosophy, physics, psychology, and anthropology to reveal why the present moment is so difficult to define. Each field offers its own understanding of 'now': physicists grapple with relativity and the slippery nature of simultaneity, psychologists examine how our brains construct our sense of the present, and anthropologists show how different cultures conceptualize time in radically different ways. Rather than settling on a single answer, Marchant embraces the complexity, showing how these varied perspectives enrich rather than resolve the mystery.
The talk concludes with a practical turn, connecting these abstract ideas to everyday life. Marchant suggests that understanding the elusive nature of 'now' can actually help us experience it more fully—by stepping away from our habitual relationship with clock time and paying closer attention to our immediate experience. It's a story worth your time because it takes something we all think we understand—this present moment—and reveals layers of wonder hiding in plain sight, ultimately offering both intellectual stimulation and a gentle invitation to be more present in our lives.

item.title: 86-year-old BTS Grandma fulfills dream of seeing South Korean group in São Paulo: 'One of the best days of my life'
item.description:
At 86 years old, Júlia Fernandes Soares Augusto from Santos, Brazil, fulfilled a dream that bridged generations and continents. The grandmother, affectionately known as "Vovó BTS," attended a concert by the South Korean pop group BTS in São Paulo, an experience she described as one of the happiest days of her life. Her journey to K-pop fandom began when she asked her grandson Raphael to introduce her to Korean bands—it was love at first sight with BTS.
Júlia became an internet sensation after a video of her emotional reaction to receiving concert tickets went viral, gathering over three million views. Her granddaughter Beatriz had tucked the tickets inside a gift box filled with BTS merchandise, initially presented as consolation for not getting real tickets. When Júlia discovered the actual passes, her joy captured hearts across social media. On concert day, Beatriz brought her grandmother to the stadium in a wheelchair, and before the show began, Júlia looked to the sky and prayed it wouldn't rain—a prayer she felt was answered.
This story resonates because it celebrates how music transcends age and cultural boundaries. Júlia came prepared with her Army Bomb light stick, spare phone chargers to capture every moment, and layered clothing for comfort. After the show, she was already hoping for a return visit. Her genuine enthusiasm reminds us that joy, curiosity, and new passions aren't confined by birthdays—and that sometimes the most remarkable fan stories come from the most unexpected places.

item.title: Starwatch: Catch the striking trifecta of Venus, the moon and Spica at break of dawn
item.description:
Early risers around the world are in for a celestial treat this week, as three luminous objects converge in the pre-dawn sky. On the morning of November 7th, Venus, the waning crescent moon, and the star Spica will form a striking alignment visible to the naked eye, creating what astronomers call a trifecta in the eastern sky.
Venus will be the star of the show, shining with its characteristic brilliance and serving as an easy landmark for spotting the grouping. Nearby, Spica—the brightest star in the constellation Virgo—will add its own light from 250 light-years away. The slender crescent moon, just two days from its new phase and only four percent illuminated, completes the trio. Patient observers may also glimpse earthshine, a subtle phenomenon where the moon's dark portion glows faintly from sunlight reflected off our own planet. The alignment will appear low on the horizon around 6:00 AM GMT, requiring a clear view to the east-south-east, and will be visible from both the northern and southern hemispheres, though viewers in the south will see it higher in the sky.
This story offers a gentle reminder that some of nature's most striking moments require nothing more than waking up early and looking up. In a world of elaborate plans and complex technology, the simple choreography of planets, moons, and stars continues to offer wonder—free, accessible, and quietly spectacular for anyone willing to greet the dawn.

item.title: ‘They have schedules to follow’: how fast ferries can threaten endangered whales in the Mediterranean
item.description:
In the protected waters of the Pelagos sanctuary in the north-western Mediterranean, marine biologist Alice Barbarioli spots a telling mark on a sperm whale's tail—a clean cut likely left by a vessel collision. These strikes have long threatened the region's endangered whales, and new data reveals the scale of the problem. An investigation using maritime tracking information found that large passenger and cargo vessels from four major ferry companies routinely travel through this protected habitat at speeds of 15 knots or higher—velocities that almost always prove fatal to whales in the event of a collision. Slowing to below 10 knots dramatically reduces lethality, yet the voluntary speed recommendations introduced in 2023 appear largely ignored.
The numbers tell a stark story. Ships spent more than 280,000 hours traveling at dangerous speeds through the particularly sensitive sea area in 2025, with some ferries exceeding 25 knots. Just seven vessels—four from Baleària and three from Grimaldi—accounted for 70% of the fastest travel times. Six ship captains, speaking candidly, explained that without binding regulations, commercial pressures make compliance nearly impossible. "They have schedules to follow," one Grimaldi captain noted, pointing to the tourism industry's tight timetables. The companies named in the investigation did not respond to requests for comment.
This story matters because it illuminates a quiet collision between conservation ideals and commercial realities. The Mediterranean hosts two-thirds of the region's fin whales and more than a fifth of its sperm whales in these waters, yet voluntary protections seem insufficient against the momentum of global trade and tourism. It's a reminder that saving endangered species often requires more than good intentions—it demands accountability.

item.title: Tens of thousands build 108 Buddhist stupas for Bhutan ‘mindfulness’ city
item.description:
In a remarkable display of collective effort, more than 40,000 volunteers in Bhutan worked through the night to construct 108 Buddhist stupas along a 12-kilometer stretch of riverbank near the Indian border. The 15-meter-tall sacred monuments, built as "a physical form of prayer made permanent in stone and earth," mark the site of Gelephu Mindfulness City, an ambitious project conceived by King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck. Nearly 200,000 people—roughly a quarter of Bhutan's entire population—attended Sunday's ceremony, underscoring the national significance of the undertaking.
The mindfulness city represents Bhutan's response to pressing economic challenges, including high unemployment, declining birth rates, and the emigration of skilled workers. Designed by Danish architects, the project aims to transform a small town of 10,000 into a vibrant hub for sustainable business, green technology, education, and tourism. The initiative reflects Bhutan's distinctive approach to development, balancing its famous "Gross National Happiness" philosophy with economic necessity. The project has attracted significant investment, including from Indian billionaire Gautam Adani, and will connect to India's rail network, with an international airport planned for 2029. Bhutan also intends to leverage its cryptocurrency holdings, earned through Bitcoin mining using surplus hydropower, to support the city's development.
This story captures a nation at a crossroads, seeking to preserve its cultural identity while adapting to modern economic realities. The image of tens of thousands building sacred structures together through the night speaks to both Bhutan's spiritual traditions and its hopes for the future—a quiet yet profound moment of collective intention in a rapidly changing world.

item.title: What does it take to build a sexy basket man?
item.description:
When a new film required turning actor Alexander Skarsgård into a romantic lead made entirely of wicker, the filmmakers behind *Wicker* knew exactly where to turn: New Zealand's renowned Wētā Workshop. The movie, a 17th-century tale starring Olivia Colman as a fisherwoman who solves her husband problem by crafting one from basketry, presented an unusual challenge—creating a believable, expressive, and yes, attractive man woven from natural materials.
For Wētā's team, famous for creating aliens and monsters for science fiction epics, designing a romantic hero from wicker required entirely new methods. Over 18 months, prosthetic makeup designers, weavers, textile artists, and sculptors collaborated to build a costume that allowed Skarsgård's performance to shine through. The final design included nine individual facial prosthetic pieces—separate lips, cheekbones, a nose, and even tiny eyelashes made from harakeke (New Zealand flax). His body consisted of 50 woven plates stitched onto a delicate spandex mesh. The team refined their process until they could complete the actor's transformation in just 90 minutes each morning on the Budapest set, with almost no CGI involved.
What makes this story quietly remarkable is how it showcases the intersection of traditional craft and cutting-edge film artistry. The project arrived just as Wētā's team of weavers and textile artists finished work on the *Avatar* films, allowing their specialized skills to flourish in an entirely unexpected context. The result is a film that's become a surprise hit, proving that sometimes the most memorable movie magic comes not from digital effects, but from the patient, creative work of human hands.

item.title: Indigenous women connect to culture through traditional crafts
item.description:
In the Indigenous community of Woorabinda, central Queensland, a woman's chance encounter with a weaving workshop has blossomed into something far larger than a personal craft. Vivianne-Lee Watson, a Wadja Wadja woman, initially had no plans to learn weaving when she accompanied residents from the local women's shelter to a workshop six-and-a-half years ago. Yet within 24 hours of making her first bracelet, she had completed a basket. That spark of connection led her to recently leave stable employment to pursue weaving full-time, hosting free workshops that have become gathering places for her community.
The workshops offer more than skill-building. For participants, they provide a "yarning circle" — a safe, judgment-free space where women can connect, share stories, or simply sit together. For newcomers like Veronica Johnson, who moved to Woorabinda this year, the sessions have been a way to build friendships and come out of her shell. The practice also carries profound cultural significance, linking participants to Indigenous weaving traditions that stretch back tens of thousands of years, when ancestors crafted essential items from reeds, bark, and plants. For Watson, weaving has become a bridge to her own heritage, connecting her to both her Wadja Wadja and Mayi-Yapi Torres Strait Islander roots.
This story is worth attention because it captures how traditional practices can answer modern needs — for identity, community, and belonging. The quiet pride on Watson's ten-year-old daughter's face after receiving her first commission for a pair of woven earrings reminds us that cultural continuity happens not through grand gestures, but through hands working together, one stitch at a time.

item.title: Phar Lap's little-known pre-cup trip to the country
item.description:
In October 1930, just weeks before his legendary Melbourne Cup victory, champion racehorse Phar Lap spent several unhurried days in the border town of Albury, New South Wales—a little-known chapter in Australian racing history. The stopover wasn't planned as a training retreat but arose from a quirk of infrastructure: trains between Sydney and Melbourne had to change at Albury due to differing rail gauges between the states, a requirement that persisted until 1962.
Phar Lap and his devoted strapper Tommy Woodcock stayed at Sodens Hotel, a racing-world hub that had hosted at least eight other Melbourne Cup winners. Woodcock slept in the loft above the stables, as was custom, keeping close watch over "Big Red." Remarkably, despite Phar Lap's fame, no one in Albury recognized the horse during their daily walks through town. Woodcock later recalled that the horse wore out his boots and two of his shirts from Phar Lap's habit of nudging his right shoulder. A telegram from the horse's connections extended their stay, ensuring Phar Lap missed the Caulfield Cup and allowing another horse, Amounis, to win at better odds—a strategic move that disappointed bettors hoping for a double.
This story offers a tender glimpse into the bond between horse and handler, and the quieter rhythms of a bygone racing era. Woodcock later shared these memories with family friend Wayne Hinchliffe, whose family cared for him in his final years. It's a reminder that behind every legendary victory are humble moments and enduring friendships—worth remembering for their warmth and humanity.

item.title: Health Expeditioners return to Iauaretê after 22 years and begin project serving Indigenous people in Amazonas
item.description:
A medical organization called the Health Expeditioners has returned to Iauaretê, a remote Indigenous community in Brazil's Amazon region, 22 years after their very first mission there. This time, they're launching an ambitious four-year project called "Cuidar para Preservar" (Care to Preserve), bringing specialized healthcare to communities along the Upper Rio Negro. What began in 2004 as a modest effort with four doctors and 100 kilograms of supplies has grown into a sophisticated operation mobilizing 60 professionals and 20 tons of medical equipment.
The current expedition, which runs through early November, offers surgeries and care in ophthalmology, general surgery, women's health, and pediatrics. The team brings a complete mobile surgical center capable of performing cataract removals, hernia repairs, and cervical cancer screenings—procedures often unavailable in these isolated areas. Access alone presents significant challenges, requiring transport by river and overland routes to reach communities where healthcare infrastructure remains limited. The project, supported by Brazil's Amazon Fund, also includes telemedicine consultations, training for local health workers, and prosthetics for amputees through a program called Forest in Motion.
Over two decades, the Health Expeditioners have completed 58 expeditions, performing more than 11,000 surgeries and 80,000 consultations across the Amazon. This story quietly illustrates how dedicated teams are bridging vast geographic and infrastructure gaps to deliver essential care. It's a reminder that healthcare equity often requires creativity, partnership with Indigenous organizations, and a willingness to bring the hospital to the patient—not the other way around.

item.title: Revisiting zombie towns: Can you have a good life in the provinces?
item.description:
A journalist revisiting small New Zealand towns discovers unexpected vitality in places once labeled "zombie towns." In Balclutha and Tokoroa, tight-knit communities are finding their own solutions to challenges that national policies often miss.
The story follows young people at critical crossroads: a head girl leaving for university, another staying for local work without student debt, a school dropout who found his way to full-time employment through a relative's patient intervention at the local YMCA. What emerges is a portrait of communities where people aren't statistics—they're known by name. Local leaders like school principal Joyce Beck, described as having "the mana," and Julius Daniels, who catches young people "at the bottom of that hill" when they fall through institutional gaps, demonstrate how relationships and time often matter more than top-down funding. The approach is bespoke and personal: rather than forcing kids down pathways that don't fit, they look for pathways that suit each individual.
The journalist finds something quietly radical in these towns—an antidote to polarization. When the invisible hand of the market (rising dairy prices, affordable housing) combines with what he calls the "invisible fabric of society" (community care, local leadership), small towns can thrive. The irony, he notes, is that while these communities were once dismissed as dying, it's now the whole country struggling with weak productivity and youth emigration. This story matters because it suggests that some of the most effective solutions to national problems aren't policy prescriptions from Wellington, but patient, relational work happening in overlooked places.

item.title: Religious missionaries travel 9,000 km to bring glasses for children with low vision and supplies to African orphanage
item.description:
A group of Brazilian religious missionaries is embarking on a 9,000-kilometer journey from São Paulo state to Tanzania, carrying a remarkable gift: high-tech glasses designed specifically for children with low vision. The mission, coordinated by the Archdiocese of Rio Preto in partnership with Franciscan friars, aims to support an orphanage in the city of Bunda that cares for 80 children, including 16 with albinism.
The specialized glasses, valued at nearly 20,000 Brazilian reais, represent six years of development by ophthalmologist Marcelo Pádua. Using a camera system that projects real-time images onto a virtual 100-inch screen, the device electronically magnifies what's in front of the wearer, helping maximize whatever residual vision exists. For the children at the orphanage—many facing severe visual impairment linked to albinism, along with intense sun exposure and historical stigma—the technology could open new possibilities for reading, recognizing faces, and navigating daily life. The team will first test the glasses with the children to assess individual needs, and if successful, plans to launch a fundraising campaign for additional pairs.
Beyond the technology, the mission carries food supplies and aims to build a lasting bridge between Brazilian and Tanzanian communities, involving confirmation students back home in ongoing support. This story quietly illustrates how innovation meets compassion across continents—a reminder that meaningful change sometimes travels thousands of kilometers in a suitcase, powered not by headlines but by dedication to seeing and being seen.

item.title: Rare beetle that oozes substance from its knees when attacked rediscovered in Wales
item.description:
After nearly six decades of absence, the short-necked oil beetle has been rediscovered thriving in Wales, offering a hopeful chapter in the story of a creature once thought nearly lost to Britain. This peculiar insect earns its name from its compact build and a remarkable defense mechanism: when threatened, it secretes an oily yellow-orange substance from its knee joints, a strategy as unusual as the beetle's entire life cycle.
The species depends on an intricate ecological partnership to survive. Its larvae, equipped with hook-like feet, cling to solitary bees and hitch rides back to their nests, where they feast on pollen stores before emerging as adults with roughly a year to live. Only about one in 10,000 larvae reach adulthood, making any viable population precious. Habitat loss throughout the twentieth century pushed the beetle to the brink, leaving just a handful of suitable sites across the UK. While adults were spotted at Castlemartin range in Pembrokeshire in 2020 and 2022, only dead specimens were found, raising fears the population might not be sustainable. But the 2025 survey brought encouraging news: larvae distributed in patterns suggesting successful breeding from a larger group of young beetles.
This rediscovery matters because it reflects the delicate interdependence of ecosystems—the beetle's survival hinges not only on thick vegetation and flower cover but on the health of solitary bee populations. Conservation efforts at the site now support multiple endangered species sharing similar habitat needs, from the shrill carder bee to rare wildflowers. It's a quiet reminder that patience and persistence in conservation can yield surprising returns, and that even the smallest, strangest creatures play irreplaceable roles in the living world around us.

item.title: Bone marrow donor in Germany helps save 9-year-old boy with rare disease in Paraná: 'A German brother'
item.description:
A nine-year-old boy in Curitiba, Brazil, calls his bone marrow donor his "German brother" — a fitting name for Florian Weiand, the 23-year-old who saved Arthur Barão Massan's life from more than 10,000 kilometers away. Arthur was diagnosed with Fanconi anemia in August 2023, a rare genetic syndrome that causes bone marrow to fail over time. His family's search for a compatible donor ended when Florian's name came up in an international registry.
Florian had registered as a donor in 2019 after friends invited him to sign up. Four years later, he received a phone call while driving home from work. Without hesitation, he agreed to donate. In 2024, his bone marrow traveled from Germany to Brazil in less than 24 hours, and the transplant was successful. Arthur's father, who had always believed in miracles, found himself living through one. The two families couldn't communicate until two years after the procedure, but when Arthur's mother finally sent an email in May 2026, Florian spent hours crafting his reply, moved by the knowledge that he had helped a child across the world continue dreaming and fighting for life.
This story is a quiet testament to the power of small decisions and invisible threads that connect strangers. Florian's simple "yes" on an ordinary commute became Arthur's second chance at a healthy childhood. Now the two families dream of the day they'll meet in person — to hug tightly, celebrate life, and perhaps play a round of Pokémon cards together. It's a reminder that compassion knows no borders, and that registering as a donor might one day mean everything to someone you'll never expect to meet.

item.title: Doctor begins working at maternity hospital where her mother has worked as general services assistant for 23 years: 'Very moving'
item.description:
In Recife, Brazil, a young obstetrician has begun working at the same maternity hospital where her mother has cleaned and maintained facilities for 23 years. Dr. Patrícia Lima recently passed a competitive public health exam and, when given the choice of placement, immediately selected the Professor Arnaldo Marques Maternity Clinic—the very place her mother Edilene's work made her medical career possible.
Patrícia was the first in her family to attend university. Her mother, who completed only six years of formal schooling, worked cleaning jobs before securing the hospital position that brought stability to their household. Edilene never pushed her daughters to work or contribute financially; instead, she encouraged them to pursue their dreams and focus on education. Though she couldn't help with homework, her steady support created the foundation for both daughters to build their futures. When colleagues at the hospital spotted Patrícia's name on the new hire list, word spread quickly, spoiling the surprise she'd hoped to deliver personally. On their first shared shift, mother and daughter walked the hospital corridors hand in hand while longtime staff members who'd watched Patrícia grow up approached them with tears and memories.
This story resonates because it illustrates how opportunity and dignity in work—even work society often overlooks—can transform across generations. It's a quiet testament to a mother's sacrifice, a daughter's determination, and the full circle that happens when both values are honored in the same place, 23 years apart.

item.title: ‘Like Kashmir’: How a toxic marble dump yard became a tourist spot in India
item.description:
In the arid landscape of Rajasthan, India, an unusual tourist attraction has emerged: a massive marble slurry dumping yard that resembles a snow-covered wonderland. The 300-acre site in Kishangarh, the largest of its kind in Asia, features pristine white hills and blue artificial lakes created from industrial waste. Hundreds of visitors flock daily to this free attraction, drawn by its surreal beauty. Newlyweds pose for photos, influencers create content, and film crews use it as a backdrop—many comparing it to the picturesque valleys of Kashmir.
Beneath the photogenic surface lies a troubling reality for the nearly 5,000 people living in surrounding villages. Kishangarh serves as a major marble and granite processing hub, home to roughly 1,200 units that generate an estimated $1.7 million in daily business. Each day, about 1,000 tankers dump approximately 5,500 tonnes of slurry waste at the government-designated site. For residents like Bagharam Gurjar and his neighbors across at least six villages, the yard has become a severe health hazard. Chronic coughs, chest infections, skin allergies, and dental problems plague the community, affecting everyone from children to the elderly. Local physicians report a significant increase in respiratory issues over recent years, with workers in marble processing units facing the greatest risks from prolonged toxic dust exposure.
This story captures a stark contradiction of modern life: what appears beautiful and Instagram-worthy to outsiders represents daily suffering for those who must live alongside it. It quietly asks us to look beyond surfaces and consider who pays the price for industry, tourism, and our curated moments of beauty.

item.title: Honest obits: 'Rolling joints, reading dirty magazines, fishing off a pier'
item.description:
Mary McGreevy has found an unexpected way to celebrate humanity's beautiful messiness. Two years ago, she launched a TikTok account called Tips from Dead People, where she shares obituaries that reject the polished, resume-style tributes in favor of something more honest and deeply human. These aren't the sanitized summaries of achievements and awards—they're vivid portraits of people in all their contradictory glory.
The obituaries McGreevy highlights capture life's delightful paradoxes. There's Renee, who couldn't cook or clean but excelled at "rolling joints, reading dirty magazines, fishing off a pier." There's Trish, remembered through a loving catalog of specifics: her adoration of Vanity Fair and cold potatoes, her hatred of hard butter and gray roots. And Kenny, a self-proclaimed "redneck SOB" who "took the idea of being hard to love as a personal challenge" yet remained deeply loved by his family despite—or perhaps because of—his flaws. McGreevy even wrote one for her own mother, noting her love of collecting cookbooks and hatred of cooking.
What makes these obituaries powerful is their refusal to airbrush reality. They understand that grief doesn't call for a LinkedIn profile at 3 a.m.—it calls for the truth of who someone really was. These portraits, oozing with affection despite their unflinching honesty, suggest that being remembered authentically might matter more than being remembered perfectly. In celebrating the Renees, Kennys, and Trishes of the world, McGreevy offers a quietly radical idea: that our contradictions and complications aren't flaws to hide, but the very things that make us unforgettable.

item.title: The unexpected neighbourhood pest terrorising this pensioner
item.description:
In the suburb of Bluewater on Townsville's outskirts, pensioner Mal Richards faces an unusual daily challenge: Eric, a friendly but persistent female emu who has claimed his property as her territory. For nine months, the beady-eyed bird has been waiting at his driveway each morning, following him around his garden, honking throughout the day, and leaving unwelcome deposits on his property. Despite Mr Richards securing his fence, Eric always finds a way through, and the retiree worries about the bird's powerful kick.
Eric appears to be a former pet emu, which explains her unusually sociable behavior with humans. While Mr Richards has contacted multiple government departments seeking help, authorities have deemed Eric's behavior non-threatening and advised residents simply to give her space and avoid feeding her. Local laws permit keeping emus on larger properties, provided they're properly enclosed—though Eric's owner remains somewhat mysterious in the reporting. The wider community has embraced Eric as a beloved local mascot, with the neighborhood Facebook page filled with sighting posts and warnings for drivers. Wildlife educator Jackie Hasling calls Eric "a little legend," though she acknowledges the daily frustrations of unwanted emu companionship.
This story captures the sometimes-awkward reality of living alongside wildlife in regional Australia, where the line between wild, domestic, and suburban can blur in unexpected ways. It's a gentle reminder that not all neighborhood disputes involve noisy parties or boundary fences—sometimes they involve a determined flightless bird with a talent for fence-hopping and an apparent fondness for one particular pensioner's morning routine.

item.title: Losing our baby shaped us in ways we never expected
item.description:
Robert Yeomans and Heidy Perez Perez met through a language-learning app in Adelaide, where Robert was studying Spanish and Heidy was an international student. After an initial meeting that didn't quite click, they reconnected a year later and built a life together, marrying in 2021. Just months after their wedding, they discovered they were expecting their first child, Thiago, conceived on Valentine's Day—a baby born of their love.
At 28 weeks, doctors discovered Thiago wasn't growing properly due to placental issues. On their wedding anniversary, Heidy woke in pain, and at the hospital they received devastating news: Thiago's heartbeat could no longer be detected. Heidy gave birth to him later that day via C-section. The loss tested their relationship profoundly, as they each grieved differently while trying to support one another through unimaginable pain. They learned that loving someone through grief doesn't always mean having the right words—sometimes it simply means being present, listening, and holding space for each other's sorrow.
This is a story about how love adapts and deepens through tragedy. Robert and Heidy describe not moving past their grief, but growing around it—becoming more compassionate, understanding, and aware of how precious their time together is. Thiago remains part of their family story, carried forward in how they love and see the world, even as they've welcomed their daughter Sienna. It's a quietly powerful reminder that resilience in relationships isn't about strength without pain, but about choosing to hold onto each other through it.

item.title: "I don't paint fat people": what lies behind the unique style of celebrated Colombian artist Fernando Botero
item.description:
Fernando Botero, the celebrated Colombian artist who passed away in 2023, created one of the most instantly recognizable styles in modern art. His voluminous figures and objects—rounded bodies, oversized heads, small features—define what has come to be known as "Boterismo." Despite popular perception, Botero insisted he didn't paint fat people; rather, he was exaggerating form to celebrate "the presence of things" and the sensuality of life itself.
The origins of his signature style trace back to a happy accident in 1956 Mexico City. While painting a mandolin, Botero drew the sound hole too small, and suddenly the instrument appeared to swell with unexpected volume and presence. From that moment, he committed to creating an entire universe governed by this aesthetic principle. His reinterpretations of masterworks—including his own version of the Mona Lisa—placed him in conversation with European art history while establishing a distinctly Latin American voice. His work achieved remarkable commercial and critical success, from MoMA acquisitions to bronze sculptures gracing Park Avenue and the Champs-Élysées.
What makes Botero's story quietly remarkable is his clarity of purpose: he believed art's fundamental job was to create pleasure and lift the spirits of those who encountered it. Through exaggerated form and vibrant color, he built a visual language that was both accessible and sophisticated, playful yet rooted in art historical tradition. His donation of his personal collection—including works by Picasso, Monet, and Dalí—to Colombia's Museo Botero wasn't mere generosity; it was a declaration that his name belonged alongside the masters who inspired him.

item.title: 'I'm 96 and TikTok pays my bills': the 'grandmas' who are dominating social media
item.description:
At 96, Lillian Droniak has found an unexpected path to financial independence: TikTok fame. Known as "Grandma Droniak" to her 15 million followers, she earns enough from social media to cover her $12,000 monthly assisted living expenses—and still sets aside money for her great-grandchildren's college funds. She's part of a growing wave of older women who have become unlikely internet celebrities, capturing the attention of audiences young enough to be their grandchildren. Droniak's journey began in 2020 when her grandson started helping her post videos out of boredom, and it has since blossomed into a business featuring brand partnerships with food and beauty companies.
Across the Atlantic, 82-year-old Viv Truran from Wales started posting colorful fashion content on Instagram after losing her husband. Now she films two videos daily from her bedroom-turned-studio, showcasing her vibrant wardrobe, 22 pairs of glasses, and drawer full of scarves. She carefully tracks her followers in notebooks—already on her fifth volume—and selectively works with brands that align with her values, including local charities. Both women say younger followers often approach them expressing fear about aging, to which they respond with the same reassuring message: getting older isn't so bad.
These stories illuminate something quietly revolutionary about digital culture—how it's creating space for voices traditionally absent from media, while also providing older adults with community, purpose, and income. Marketing experts note that these creators offer brands access to deeply loyal audiences with real purchasing power, but perhaps more meaningful is how they're reshaping perceptions about aging itself, one post at a time.

item.title: Sea turtles' favourite Kiwi hangouts revealed
item.description:
Satellite tracking technology is revealing the secret lives of green sea turtles visiting New Zealand waters, and the findings are reshaping what researchers know about these ocean travelers. Eleven rehabilitated turtles fitted with temporary satellite tags have shown surprising mobility and clear habitat preferences, offering a window into their mysterious routines without human interference.
The tracked turtles have demonstrated a particular fondness for certain locations in Northland—including Rangaunu Bay, Pārengarenga Harbour, and the Bay of Islands—as well as Auckland's Manukau Harbour, where one turtle made a month-long stopover. While some turtles settle into a single harbour for extended periods, others embark on impressive journeys. One adventurous individual traveled all the way to Wellington and back to Northland, possibly in search of food. These movements have confirmed that New Zealand serves as a kind of "baby-sitting service for teenagers"—a temporary home for young turtles before they eventually depart to breed elsewhere across the Pacific.
Beyond the charming revelation of turtle "zoomies," the research carries practical importance. Recent months have seen an uptick in unwell turtles arriving at facilities, many suffering from boat strikes, fishing line entanglements, and illnesses possibly linked to environmental degradation and reduced food access. The tracking data is helping conservationists identify critical habitats worth protecting and offering boaters practical guidance—like appointing lookouts, adding propeller guards, and slowing down in turtle-frequented waters. This story matters because it demonstrates how technology can illuminate the hidden patterns of marine life while pointing toward tangible ways humans can share the ocean more safely with its ancient inhabitants.

item.title: Santos has film, choro, and literature festivals during extended holiday; see the schedule
item.description:
The coastal city of Santos, São Paulo, is offering residents and visitors a rich cultural menu over Brazil's extended Day of the Dead holiday weekend. The programming spans music, film, and literature — all with an emphasis on accessibility and tradition.
The inaugural Chororô Festival celebrates choro, a characteristically Brazilian musical genre known for its intricate melodies and improvisational spirit. The day-long event includes free workshops on instruments from seven-string guitar to bandolim, culminating in performances that honor both the genre's roots and its evolution. Meanwhile, other musical offerings include the Chorinho no Aquário project, which spotlights overlooked songs from Brazil's popular music archive, and a beachfront dance event featuring Banda Imagem!. Film enthusiasts can catch horror classics at the Cinemateca in keeping with Halloween, or explore Lebanese cinema at the Museum of Image and Sound. The 18th edition of the Tarrafa Literária festival brings together writers, journalists, philosophers, and readers for discussions and activities aimed at all ages, while the Cidade Essencial project launches its fourth edition with performances and reflections on community and belonging.
What makes this weekend noteworthy is its deliberate weaving together of high and popular culture, old and new artistic forms, all offered freely or affordably to the public. It's a reminder that civic cultural programming can be both ambitious and inclusive, turning a holiday weekend into an opportunity for discovery and connection across generations and interests.

item.title: Amazônia Imersiva Crosses the Atlantic and Brings Contemporary Amazonian Art to Portugal
item.description:
For centuries, the Amazon was depicted in Europe through the eyes of travelers and colonizers. Now, artists from the region itself are bringing their own perspectives across the Atlantic. Amazonia Immersive Art, created in Belém, Brazil, has opened its first international exhibition in Porto, Portugal, transforming paintings, photographs, and videos into monumental projections. Under the artistic direction of Roberta Carvalho and Aíla, both from the Amazon state of Pará, the show runs at Casa das Máquinas through April 2027.
The exhibition weaves together contemporary art, ancestral knowledge, and digital technology across three carefully curated rooms. The first explores connections between forest and people, questioning the separation between nature and culture. The second features immersive projections from seven artists and collectives—including the MAHKU collective of Huni Kuin Indigenous artists, photographer Elza Lima, and Peruvian Shipibo-Konibo artist Olinda Silvano—whose works span different generations and Indigenous nations. The final room centers on ancestrality and listening, showcasing work from writer Ailton Krenak (the first Indigenous member of the Brazilian Academy of Letters), visual artist Keila Sankofa, the late Makuxi artist Jaider Esbell, and master ceramicist Ronaldo Guedes, accompanied by a chant in the Tikuna language.
